name: Nayirah

summary.text: 'Nayirah' was the name under which a 15-year-old Kuwaiti girl testified on October 10, 1990 before the Congressional Human Rights Caucus, co-chaired by Reps. Tom Lantos and John Porter, that she had seen Iraqi soldiers remove infants from incubators in a Kuwait City hospital. Her testimony was arranged by the public-relations firm Hill & Knowlton, working for Citizens for a Free Kuwait, a Kuwaiti-government-funded campaign. In 1992 it emerged that she was Nayirah al-Sabah, daughter of Kuwait's ambassador to the United States, Saud Nasir al-Sabah; human-rights investigators later could not substantiate the incubator account.

facts.claim: On October 10, 1990 a 15-year-old Kuwaiti girl identified only as Nayirah testified before the Congressional Human Rights Caucus that she had personally seen Iraqi forces take infants from incubators; Rep. Tom Lantos said her identity was withheld to protect her family.

sources.title: A Debate On One Of The Most Infamous Pieces of Propaganda: The Nayirah Testimony

facts.claim: Hill & Knowlton, working with Reps. Lantos and Porter, introduced Nayirah at the hearing; according to John MacArthur's book Second Front, the firm had prepared her for the presentation.
facts.quote: H&K had prepped Nayirah for her presentation

facts.claim: In 1992 it was revealed that Nayirah's surname was al-Sabah and that she was the daughter of Saud Nasir al-Sabah, Kuwait's ambassador to the United States.

sources.title: A Debate On One Of The Most Infamous Pieces of Propaganda: The Nayirah Testimony

facts.claim: Citizens for a Free Kuwait was a campaign established by the Kuwaiti government to win American support for military action, and Hill & Knowlton was its main contractor.
facts.quote: a Kuwaiti government-established campaign to win American favor for military action, and its main contractor was Hill & Knowlton

facts.claim: President George H.W. Bush repeatedly cited the incubator allegations, and several senators used them in debate on the January 1991 resolution authorising force; later investigations by Amnesty International, Physicians for Human Rights and others could not document the incubator claims, and Amnesty retracted its earlier report in 1991.
facts.quote: When human rights organizations investigated, they could not find any connection between Nayirah and the hospital.

openQuestions: The site's headline calls the testimony 'invented'. Sources found say investigators could not substantiate the incubator account and that Nayirah was the ambassador's daughter; whether she fabricated or repeated what she was told is contested, and the 1992 ABC 20/20 and New York Times reports the site cites were not reachable.
The Congressional Human Rights Caucus was not a formal committee, so there is no official hearing transcript in the congressional record; the owner may wish to cite C-SPAN's video archive.
